title: Saturn and Its Rings
summary: What Saturn is made of, what its famous rings are, how Galileo first saw them, and facts about its moons, days, and years.
poll: Saturn is the most interesting planet in our solar system.

versions.title: The Ring Planet
versions.text:
Look up at night. Do you see a bright dot? It may be Saturn. It does not twinkle. It is a planet. It goes round the sun. So do we. It is the sixth one out from the sun.

Saturn is huge. Just one is more big. That one is Jupiter. Saturn is not rock, like Earth. It is gas. There is no ground to stand on. It is so light! It could float in a tub of water. But the tub would have to be so big!

Saturn has rings. They go all the way round it. The rings are bits of ice and rock. Some bits are as small as dust. Some are as big as a house. The rings are wide. But they are thin.

Long ago, a man named Galileo had a telescope. He saw the rings. He did not know what they were. He thought they were ears!

Saturn has lots of moons. The big one is Titan. It is more big than the planet Mercury.

A day there is short. It is just ten or so hours. But a year is long. It is as long as twenty-nine of our years!

On a clear night, you might see a bright dot in the sky that does not twinkle. It could be Saturn. Saturn is a planet, and like Earth, it travels around the sun. It is the sixth planet from the sun. It is about ten times as far from the sun as we are.

Saturn is so light for its size that it could float in water. You would just need a bathtub big enough to hold it!

About four hundred years ago, a scientist named Galileo looked at Saturn through a telescope. He saw the rings, but he could not tell what they were. He thought Saturn might have two big ears!

Saturn has lots of moons. Its biggest moon, Titan, is even larger than the planet Mercury.

A day on Saturn is short. It lasts only about ten and a half hours. But a year there is very long. Saturn takes about twenty-nine Earth years to go once around the sun.

versions.title: Saturn: The Ringed Giant
versions.text:
On a clear night, you might notice a bright point of light that shines steadily instead of twinkling. It could be Saturn. Many people think it is the most beautiful planet. Saturn is the sixth planet from the sun, and it is about ten times farther from the sun than Earth is.

Saturn is the second largest planet. Only Jupiter is bigger. Unlike Earth, Saturn does not have a rocky surface. It is a gas giant, which means it is made mostly of gas. If you tried to land a spaceship there, you would sink into thick clouds. You would never touch solid ground. Saturn is also very light for its size. In fact, it could float in water, if anyone could find a bathtub big enough to hold it!

Saturn is famous for its rings. They are made of billions of pieces of ice and rock that orbit the planet. Some pieces are as small as grains of dust, while others are as big as a house. The rings stretch very wide around the planet, but in most places they are only about as thick as a tall building is high.

About four hundred years ago, the astronomer Galileo looked at Saturn through a simple telescope. He could see that something was next to the planet, but he could not tell what it was. He thought Saturn had two large ears! Later, with better telescopes, scientists learned that they were rings.

Saturn has many moons. The largest, Titan, is even bigger than the planet Mercury and has a thick, hazy sky.

A day on Saturn lasts only about ten and a half hours, because the planet spins very fast. But a year is very long. Saturn takes about twenty-nine Earth years to orbit the sun once.

From 2004 to 2017, a spacecraft called Cassini circled Saturn and sent back amazing pictures and facts.

Saturn is the second largest planet, surpassed in size exclusively by Jupiter. Unlike Earth, Saturn does not possess a rocky surface; instead, it is a gas giant composed predominantly of hydrogen and helium, the two lightest elements in the universe. If a spacecraft attempted to land there, it would descend progressively deeper into increasingly dense clouds without ever encountering solid ground. Because these gases are extraordinarily light, Saturn has an exceptionally low average density, and consequently it is the only planet that could theoretically float in water, provided that anyone could locate a bathtub sufficiently enormous to contain it.

Saturn is celebrated for its spectacular rings, which consist of billions of fragments of ice and rock that orbit the planet independently. Individual fragments range from minute particles of dust to enormous chunks approximately the size of a house. Although the rings extend an astonishing distance around the planet, in most locations they are only about as thick as a tall building is high.

Approximately four hundred years ago, the Italian astronomer Galileo made an observation of Saturn through a primitive telescope, and although he could perceive that something was attached to the sides of the planet, he was unable to identify it, so he speculated that Saturn might possess two large ears. Several decades later, using considerably more sophisticated telescopes, other scientists determined that these mysterious formations were actually rings.

Saturn has numerous moons, more than any other planet in the solar system. The largest, Titan, is even bigger than the planet Mercury and is enveloped by a thick, hazy atmosphere. Another moon, Enceladus, ejects geysers of icy water into space, suggesting that an extensive ocean may be concealed beneath its frozen exterior.

How to build your own telescope at home

How people traveled to Saturn
questions.why: The article describes Saturn's size, what it is made of, its rings, its moons, and its days and years.

wrong.B: A telescope is mentioned, but the article does not teach how to build one.
wrong.C: The article does not say Earth is the best planet.
wrong.D: No people have traveled to Saturn in the article.

Jupiter

wrong.A: Mercury is a planet. Titan is bigger than it.
wrong.B: Jupiter is the only planet bigger than Saturn.
wrong.C: Galileo is the man who saw the rings.

questions.stem: Galileo used a telescope to look at Saturn. What is a telescope?
options: A map of the stars
A tool that makes far things look closer
A kind of space ship
A book about planets
questions.why: Galileo used the telescope to see Saturn's rings, which are too far away to see well with just your eyes.

wrong.A: A map shows where stars are; it does not make them look closer.
wrong.C: Galileo did not fly to Saturn.
wrong.D: He looked through the telescope; he did not read it.

questions.stem: How is Saturn different from Earth?
options: Saturn is made of gas, not rock.
Saturn is much closer to the sun than Earth is.
Saturn has no moons.
Saturn is made of hard rock.
questions.why: The article says Earth is rock, but Saturn is gas with no ground.

wrong.B: Saturn is the sixth planet, farther from the sun than Earth.
wrong.D: Earth is rock; Saturn is gas.

questions.stem: Why did Galileo most likely think Saturn had ears?
options: He saw a drawing of Saturn with ears.
He heard sounds coming from Saturn.
His telescope could not show the rings clearly.
He was looking at the wrong planet.
questions.why: Galileo saw something on the sides of Saturn but could not tell what it was, so the rings must have looked blurry to him.

wrong.A: The article does not mention a drawing.
wrong.B: Planets do not have ears, and he did not hear anything.
wrong.D: He was looking at Saturn and its rings.

questions.stem: If you lived on Saturn, why would you have very few birthdays?
options: Saturn is much too cold for any birthday parties.
A day on Saturn is very short.
Saturn is far from Earth.
A Saturn year lasts about twenty-nine of ours.
questions.why: A birthday comes once a year, and one Saturn year is as long as about twenty-nine of our years.

wrong.A: The article does not talk about parties.
wrong.B: Short days do not mean fewer birthdays.
wrong.C: Distance from Earth does not change how long a year is on Saturn.

questions.stem: How does the author share information in this article?

By giving facts about Saturn in each part

By comparing every planet one by one

wrong.C: There are no steps to follow.

LOW.prompt: Which fact about Saturn surprised you the most? Write about it and tell why it surprised you.

I explained why it surprised me.

LOW.modelAnswer: The fact that surprised me most is that Saturn could float in water. I never knew a planet could be light enough to float, since it does not even have a rocky surface like Earth. This made me realize that Saturn is mostly made of gas, which is why it is so surprisingly light for its huge size.

MID.prompt: Imagine you are a scientist working with the Cassini spacecraft. Write a short report about three things you would tell people about Saturn.
checklist: I included three facts from the article about Saturn.
I explained each fact in my own words.
I organized my report with an opening and a closing sentence.
MID.modelAnswer: As a scientist on the Cassini mission, I would love to share what we learned while orbiting Saturn. First, Saturn is a gas giant with no rocky surface at all, so a spacecraft trying to land would just sink into thick clouds. Second, its famous rings are made of billions of pieces of ice and rock that range from tiny dust grains to chunks as big as a house. Third, Saturn has more moons than any other planet, and its largest moon, Titan, is even bigger than the planet Mercury. These discoveries from our spacecraft have taught us more about Saturn than anyone ever knew before.

HIGH.prompt: Scientists have studied Saturn for about four hundred years. Explain how tools such as telescopes and spacecraft have changed what we know about Saturn, using evidence from the article.
checklist: I explained how at least two tools helped scientists learn about Saturn.
I supported my explanation with specific evidence from the article.
I organized my writing with a clear introduction, body, and conclusion.
HIGH.modelAnswer: Over four hundred years, better and better tools have completely transformed our observation and understanding of Saturn. When Galileo first looked at Saturn through a simple telescope about four hundred years ago, he could only see that something odd was attached to its sides, and he mistakenly guessed the planet had two large ears. Centuries later, far more powerful telescopes let other scientists finally confirm that these were actually rings made of ice and rock. Then, from 2004 to 2017, the Cassini spacecraft flew directly to Saturn and sent back thousands of detailed pictures and measurements, revealing facts no telescope on Earth could ever have captured, such as the true size of its moon Titan. In conclusion, each new tool, from Galileo's telescope to the Cassini spacecraft, has let scientists see Saturn more clearly and accurately than the tool before it.
